title: AI in Education #6: Five Things I Learned from Dan Meyer about Why AI Should Serve Teachers, Not Replace Them
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton reports on a conversation with Dan Meyer, a former maths teacher now at Amplify who has both built AI features for classrooms and publicly criticized AI tutoring hype. Meyer argues AI tutors have failed to deliver because the decisions involved in real tutoring — when to intervene, when to hold back, what a student needs given their history — are social as well as cognitive, and no platform has solved even the basic timing problem, pointing to Khan Academy's own admission that Khanmigo isn't doing what they expected. The AI features that do work, like Amplify's Discussion Moments, make the teacher-student relationship stronger rather than weaker by having AI process student responses at scale and hand the relational work back to the teacher. Meyer also raises the '95/5 problem': AI tutoring efficacy studies typically show gains only for the small fraction of students already motivated enough to engage, leaving the students who need help most unserved. His closing provocation is that AI is all potential energy and no kinetic energy, and its outsized share of the education conversation may be sustained by people with a financial stake in keeping it there.
points: AI tutors cannot solve the timing problem — knowing when to offer help, hold back, or intervene draws on everything a teacher knows about a student's social and cognitive history, and even Khan Academy has admitted Khanmigo isn't working as intended.

The AI features that work make teachers more present, not less: Amplify's Discussion Moments has AI process 35 free-text student responses and surface four for class discussion, keeping the relational and intellectual work with the teacher.

The 95/5 problem: efficacy studies for personalized-learning platforms typically report gains only after excluding the 90-95% of students who didn't engage enough — meaning the 'proof' comes from the population least representative of who most needs help.

An experienced teacher can catch AI errors — mismatched units, nonsensical contexts, hallucinated word problems — that a novice cannot, meaning AI multiplies teacher expertise asymmetrically rather than substituting for it.

Meyer's closing critique reframes the entire AI-in-education conversation: relative to genuinely transformative technologies, AI remains mostly potential energy, and its prominence in the discourse may be driven by the financial interests of those who benefit from the hype.
quotes: If you have ever sat beside a student and helped them through a problem, you know the decisions involved are constant and subtle. When do you intervene? When do you hold back? When does a student need encouragement, and when do they need to be told: “No, keep going, you are closer than you think”? These are not just cognitive decisions. They are social ones.

Dan pointed to Khanmigo’s struggle with something as basic as when to offer help. First, they had it off until the student clicked it. Nobody clicked. Then they triggered it when a student clicked into the answer box and clicked out. Now it is just always on. These are the largest companies in ed-tech, and they cannot solve the timing problem.
The AI does the language processing. The teacher does the work of building relationships around mathematical content.

Dan put it bluntly: Students do not care about bringing their best work to an AI chatbot. They do care about their classmates seeing them. They care when the teacher says, "Ooh, this is wrong, but very interesting." That has an effect — socially, on every single person in the classroom.

If you analyse the efficacy reports from personalised learning companies – the ones that claim their AI tutoring platform produces measurable gains - you typically find that the positive results only emerge after excluding what appears to be 90–95% of the study population. The students who did not engage enough, who did not complete enough sessions, who dropped out.

If the technology only works for 5% of students, that still leaves 95% unserved. And the 5% it works for are likely the students who were already most motivated and most capable of self-directed learning.

Relative to other technological innovations – the steam engine, the combustion engine, vaccinations, the telegraph – AI has not yet transformed the day-to-day experience of most people. It is, as Dan put it, all potential energy and no kinetic.

Dan’s hypothesis: the success of AI would generate value for a small number of people who have a lot of interest in both media properties and AI companies. And so it does not surprise him that the media talks about AI quite a lot, and that people like you and me, further downstream, find ourselves talking about it too – instead of talking about the social and political solutions that are harder but more likely to work.
